extracted.intended_audience: regulatory stakeholders, agency staff, environmental attorneys, and public commenters interested in power plant emissions rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: A paginated Federal Register API search result listing recent proposed rules, final rules, notices, and supporting materials related to 'power plant emissions.' The page aggregates document titles, abstracts, excerpts, and links relevant to regulatory requirements and standards for emissions from power plants and related facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: CAA section 111 predicate finding (GHG regulation of EGUs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the Clean Air Act (CAA) requires a finding that greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants 'contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution' as a predicate to regulating those emissions under CAA section 111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA may propose making such a finding or alternatively propose that GHG emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants do not contribute significantly; legal interpretation (including the major questions doctrine) is central to the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Implementation Plan (SIP) required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For an attainment plan/SIP submission: includes an attainment demonstration, emission limitations necessary to provide for attainment, base-year and projection-year emission inventories, reasonably available control measures and reasonably available control technology (RACM/RACT), nonattainment new source review (NNSR), requirements for meeting reasonable further progress (RFP), and contingency measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluates SIP submissions against these statutory elements under the Clean Air Act when proposing to approve or disapprove state plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion procedure for modeled SO2 hourly to 30-day rolling average limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure (per appendix C of 2014 SO2 guidance) to convert a modeled hourly SO2 emission rate to a 30-day rolling average SO2 emission limit by determining the ratio between 99th percentile emission rates for the applicable averaging time (30 days) and 1-hour 99th percentile emission rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State first determines a modeled hourly SO2 emission rate (example given: 6,412.80 lb/hr) and uses percentile ratio methodology to derive longer-term averaging limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit-based emission limits and monitoring (facility-specific limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Source-specific emission limits for power plants (e.g., SO2 limits in a Permit to Install) and demonstration that monitored emission-rate averages (monthly, quarterly, etc.) are within permit limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may submit modeled analyses demonstrating that permit emission limits, in combination with other factors (e.g., plant shutdowns, background concentrations), yield compliance with NAAQS or other standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably Available Control Technology (RACT) demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: A State's demonstration that the control options in a source-specific SIP revision implement Reasonably Available Control Technology (RACT) for pollutants such as NOx for affected facility sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluates whether submitted emission limits implement RACT by considering the demonstrated control options, feasibility, and whether additional controls are available or necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Available Control Technology / Lowest Achievable Emission Rate (BACT/LAER) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination that certain control combinations (e.g., low-NOx burners with SCR and use of low-sulfur oil plus SCR) are considered BACT/LAER for purposes of permitting and emissions control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA/State may conclude certain control packages meet BACT/LAER based on technical demonstrations and permitting analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems (CEMS) monitoring and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions are monitored via CEMS, reported on a semi-annual basis (or other specified intervals), and data are maintained for specified durations (e.g., up to five years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEMS operation, reporting frequency, and record retention are used to demonstrate ongoing compliance with emission limits and SIP/permit conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of NEPA issues for nuclear license renewal (Category 1 vs Category 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The LR GEIS defines which environmental impacts are generic (Category 1) and which impacts are plant-specific (Category 2) and require a plant-specific analysis during license renewal NEPA review; determinations are codified in Table B-1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1 issues are generally considered bound by GEIS findings; Category 2 issues require site-specific analysis in the environmental review for license renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum Achievable Control Technology (MACT) standards for HAPs
rubrics_metrics.description: MACT standards set emission limitations for hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) such as hydrogen chloride (HCl), mercury, organic HAPs, and dioxin/furans for specified source categories (example: lime manufacturing plants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rulemaking may establish pollutant-specific MACT limits and related compliance obligations to achieve reductions in tons/year or pounds/year as quantified in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fPM as a surrogate for non-mercury HAP metals (MATS context)
rubrics_metrics.description: A filterable particulate matter (fPM) emission standard can serve as a surrogate measure for non-mercury hazardous air pollutant metals for existing coal-fired EGUs; associated compliance demonstration requirements and mercury standards may be specified (including subcategory-specific standards such as for lignite-fired EGUs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule language may set fPM limits, specify how compliance is demonstrated, and identify subcategory-specific pollutant standards to be applied or repealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental Assessment (EA) / Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) requirements for power plant actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies prepare EAs and FONSIs (or EISs if significant impacts are expected) evaluating environmental impacts of federal actions related to power plant operations, license transfers, exemptions, or financial support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and final EAs/FONSIs are documented and made available for public review; supporting correspondence and RAI responses may be included in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: CAA section 112 technology review and decision to regulate previously unregulated emission points
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a technology review pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6), EPA may determine whether to revise NESHAP to regulate previously unregulated emission points (e.g., acid gas removal units, loading operations, storage vessels) or to defer regulation of those points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may propose alternative approaches (no obligation to regulate vs. new control standards) and seek comment; the review can also include technical corrections and definitional changes (e.g., 'associated equipment').

rubrics_metrics.name: State delegation of NSPS/NESHAP via incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: State environmental agencies may seek delegation/approval to implement NSPS/NESHAP by incorporating by reference federal standards as promulgated through a specific effective date (example: 'as they existed through July 1, 2021' or 'June 30, 2023').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluates state regulatory updates, the scope of delegation (which sources/areas are covered), and any applicability exclusions (e.g., Indian country).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustments to emissions budgets and allowance allocations (CSAPR context)
rubrics_metrics.description: State emissions budgets and default unit-level allocations of emission allowances (e.g., for NOx during the ozone season) may be adjusted to account for changes such as deferred or cancelled retirement plans of electricity generating units (EGUs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may revise budgets and allocations when underlying assumptions (like announced retirements) change, affecting the emissions baseline used in rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of opacity/excess emissions and monthly emission-rate averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilities submit periodic reports (e.g., quarterly Opacity Excess Emissions Reports) that include monthly SO2 emission-rate averages and other monitoring data; these reports are used to demonstrate compliance with permit limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory approvals reference these reporting schedules and use the reported averages to evaluate ongoing compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: EIS evaluation criteria for new generation projects (purpose and need, reliability, integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: An EIS evaluates alternatives against the project's purpose and need (e.g., supporting load growth), reliability and resiliency objectives, provision of dispatchable/firm generation capacity, planning reserve margin targets, and ability to integrate renewables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of a preferred alternative is informed by consistency with integrated resource plans, operational flexibility, and system reliability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal interpretive standards (major questions doctrine / statutory interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating agency authority to regulate (e.g., rescission of GHG endangerment findings), legal tests such as the major questions doctrine and statutory construction principles (e.g., clear statement rules) are used to determine whether statutory provisions authorize broad regulatory actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory actions may rest on multiple legal bases, including interpretation of terms like 'air pollution,' 'cause,' and 'contribute,' and courts' treatment (e.g., West Virginia v. EPA) can shape rulemaking outcomes.
